# Sub-course · Design in the Literature

> **Reading published studies backwards: from the methods section to the design**
> [Main course](../../README.md) · [Module 1 — Breeding and Agronomy →](01-breeding-and-agronomy.md) · [Module 2](02-molecular-and-cell-biology.md) · [Module 3](03-clinical-and-preclinical.md) · [Module 4](04-omics-and-bioinformatics.md) · [Module 5](05-ecology-and-microbiome.md) · [Module 6](06-neuroscience.md) · [Module 7](07-biotech-and-bioprocess.md) · [Module 8](08-pharmacy.md)

---

**Eighty open-access papers, ten per field, each read backwards from its methods section.**

The main course teaches design **forwards**: question → unit → allocation → size → analysis.
Real life mostly runs **backwards**. A paper lands on your desk, and you have to work out what
was actually done, whether the design supports the claim in the abstract, and what you would
do differently.

That is the skill this sub-course trains, on **real, open-access papers**. Each case links to
its full text and DOI. Excerpts provide a starting point; the diagrams and “Reading it” sections
are teaching interpretations that you should check against the source. Brackets and omissions in
excerpts indicate editorial interventions. An interpretation can be reasonable without being an
explicit statement by the authors.

## Choose a learning route

This companion is aimed at senior undergraduates, graduate students, researchers and interested
readers. Familiarity with the main course's [units and replication](../../chapters/03-experimental-unit-and-replication.md),
[randomization](../../chapters/04-randomization-and-blinding.md),
[blocking](../../chapters/05-blocking-and-batches.md) and
[question types](../../chapters/02-start-with-the-question.md) will help.

You do not need to read all eighty papers in sequence. Start with the field closest to your work:

1. **Guided case:** Audit Paper 1 using the worksheet below, then expand “Reading it” to compare.
2. **Independent case:** Pick another paper in that module. Open its full text first; write your
   audit before reading either the course diagram or its interpretation.
3. **Transfer:** Complete the module's independent transfer task, then audit a case in another field.
   Explain which design principle transfers and which practical constraint changes.

The remaining cases form a reference library for seminars and research planning. Protocols describe
planned procedures, simulations support conclusions conditional on their assumptions, and reviews
summarize reported evidence. They are not interchangeable with completed intervention studies.

## Evidence worksheet

Copy this table for a paper. Add a section, page, table or figure locator in the evidence column.
Label each statement **reported**, **inferred**, or **not reported**. “Not reported” does not mean
“not done”; use it to mark an uncertainty rather than to invent a procedure or assert misconduct.

| Item | Your answer | Source evidence and status |
|---|---|---|
| Question and target | Population, outcome, contrast and intended use | |
| Study status | Completed study, protocol, simulation, benchmark or review | |
| Units and counts | Assignment, sampling and measurement units; counts for each outcome | |
| Allocation and measurement | Randomization, blocking, masking, standardization and their stages | |
| Controls | Alternative explanation addressed; alternatives still open | |
| Data structure and analysis | Pairing, nesting, repeated measures, batches and missingness | |
| Warranted conclusion | Effect estimate and uncertainty; scope of generalization | |
| Feasible redesign | One change, constraint, cost or trade-off | |

Draw the hierarchy yourself. A course diagram is a schematic reconstruction, not proof that
an allocation procedure occurred. Distinguish independent units from records, wells, cells and
technical repeats; denominators may change between outcomes.

Assess each audit on four criteria: **traceable evidence**, **correct units and comparisons**,
**calibrated conclusions**, and **a feasible redesign with a trade-off**. An answer that identifies
an unresolved fact with a precise source question can be stronger than a confident guess. Sample
answers are examples, not a universal ten-point marking scheme.

## How each paper is handled

| Step | The question you answer |
|---|---|
| **1 · Question** | What is being asked, and which of the eight types is it? |
| **2 · Unit** | What was the treatment assigned to? Is the reported *n* counted in those units? |
| **3 · Allocation** | Randomized? Blocked? Blinded? Or simply not stated? |
| **4 · Controls** | Which alternative explanations are closed off, and which are left open? |
| **5 · Analysis** | Does the model mirror the layout — blocks, nesting, repeated measures? |
| **6 · Supports** | What does this design genuinely support? |
| **7 · Redesign** | One change you would make, under a stated constraint |

## A note on tone

These papers were chosen because their methods are **clearly enough reported to be read**,
which is a compliment, not an accusation. Where a design has a limit, that limit is a teaching
point about the design — not a judgement of the researchers, who worked under constraints of
land, animals, budget and season that the reader does not see.

## Modules

| # | Module | Papers | Designs covered |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Breeding and Agronomy](01-breeding-and-agronomy.md) | 10 | factorial in blocks · α-lattice · multi-environment trials · genomic prediction · animal feeding trial · mass mating and pseudo-pedigrees · repeated records and contemporary groups · a simulation with a control arm · reference-set composition · strategy benchmarking |
| 2 | [Molecular and Cell Biology](02-molecular-and-cell-biology.md) | 10 | reporting *n* at the bench · knockdown specificity · validating normalizers · sub-sampling and blinding · a strain panel as a factorial · antibody validation · selection in a biobank · a pooled screen through a bottleneck · a cell panel as a design · endpoints chosen by a pathway |
| 3 | [Clinical and Preclinical](03-clinical-and-preclinical.md) | 10 | concealment vs blinding · cluster randomization · crossover and washout · the CONSORT flow · an ARRIVE-reported animal study · stepped wedge · where ICCs come from · pre-specified adaptation · target trial emulation · a preclinical literature under a bias tool |
| 4 | [Omics and Bioinformatics](04-omics-and-bioinformatics.md) | 10 | cells vs donors and pseudobulk · dose–response with pooling · an incomplete factorial · a measurement-validation ladder · nested cross-validation · constructing ground truth · analytic choices that propagate · independent benchmarking · randomized plexes with a bridge · validating across compartments |
| 5 | [Ecology and the Microbiome](05-ecology-and-microbiome.md) | 10 | split-plot in the field · replicate populations · randomizing wild animals · randomized extraction batches · a confound the authors name · BACI · natural experiments · reciprocal transplants · imperfect detection · space-for-time tested |
| 6 | [Neuroscience](06-neuroscience.md) | 10 | litters and cells as units · counterbalancing · opsin-negative controls · within-subject crossover · power and preregistration across a field · sex as a design factor · group effect vs individual reliability |
| 7 | [Biotechnology and Bioprocess](07-biotech-and-bioprocess.md) | 10 | screening designs and aliasing · centre points and pure error · response surfaces · confirmation runs · OFAT as range-finding · scale-up under constraint · validating the instrument |
| 8 | [Pharmacy](08-pharmacy.md) | 10 | bioequivalence crossovers · replicate designs for variable drugs · equivalence margins · factorial and split-plot stability studies · AQbD method design · inter-laboratory ring studies · cluster trials and evidence synthesis |

Each module stands alone, so you can start with the field closest to your own work. The main course's
[capstone](../../chapters/26-capstone-design-clinic.md) then asks you to design your own study.
